interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the pump shaft's speed fall and torque rise by one ratio, while the teeth share one speed at the mesh and the power passes through, when you add teeth to the wheel.
interactive.title: The gear pair
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: The picture runs over thirteen small screens. The main picture is a gear pair. An 11 kW motor turns at 1450 rev/min, which is 151.8 rad/s. On its shaft is a small gear, the pinion. It meshes with a bigger gear, the wheel, on the pump's shaft. Every tooth is the same size, 4 mm of diameter for each tooth. So the 20-tooth pinion is 80 mm across and the 100-tooth wheel is 400 mm across. Dragging a gear's rim in or out changes its tooth count, and its size grows with it. The pinion runs from 12 to 40 teeth and opens at 20. The wheel runs from 12 to 120 teeth and opens at 100. An efficiency slider runs from 80% to 100% in 1% steps and opens at an example 95%. Each shaft carries a speed arrow and a torque arrow, drawn to scale. A dot sits where the teeth meet. It is labelled with the speed of both gears' teeth there, 6.1 m/s at the opening settings. That is the pinion's 151.8 rad/s × its 0.04 m radius, and the wheel's 30.4 rad/s × its 0.2 m radius. A power bar runs from the motor, through the mesh, to the pump. It starts at 11 kW and comes out smaller by the loss, shaded at the mesh. The rule the picture computes is this. The wheel turns slower than the pinion by the gear ratio, the wheel's teeth ÷ the pinion's teeth. The motor's torque is 11,000 W ÷ 151.8 rad/s = 72.4 N m. The pump shaft's torque is the motor's torque × the ratio × the efficiency. The power out is the power in × the efficiency. At the opening settings the ratio is 100 ÷ 20 = 5. The pump shaft turns at 1450 ÷ 5 = 290 rev/min and carries 72.4 × 5 × 0.95 = 344 N m. The power out is 10.45 kW, so 550 W turns to heat. At 100% efficiency the pump shaft carries 362 N m and the power out is the full 11 kW. With equal teeth on both gears, the speed and torque pass through unchanged, less the loss. With the wheel smaller than the pinion, the pump shaft speeds up and its torque falls. The two gears turn opposite ways, and their arrows show it. Readouts give the pump shaft's speed in rev/min, its torque in N m and the power out in kW. On a narrow phone the three readouts wrap onto two lines. The gears turn 50 times slower than real, and the readouts give real speeds. A Second pair switch adds a compound train. A second 20-tooth pinion on the wheel's shaft drives a 60-tooth wheel, and the pump moves onto that last shaft. Its ratio is 3, so the whole train's ratio is 5 × 3 = 15. The pump shaft then turns at 96.7 rev/min. Each pair loses its own share, so at 95% each the train passes about 90%, 9.93 kW, and the pump shaft carries 981 N m. Two meshes turn the last shaft the same way as the motor. A Belt switch swaps the first gear pair for two pulleys and a belt, with the same diameters: 80 mm and 400 mm at the opening settings. The rim drags then set the pulley diameters, 4 mm for each step. A dot on the belt shows it moving at the speed of both pulley rims, 6.1 m/s. The belt is an open one, so both pulleys turn the same way. Screen 1 shows the opening gear pair turning. It reminds you of a 5 : 1 reduction as a ratio of speeds, 1450 rev/min in and 290 rev/min out. The mesh dot shows why. Each tooth that passes the mesh on the pinion pushes one tooth past on the wheel, so the pinion turns five times for one turn of the wheel. Screen 2 asks the wheel's speed when a 15-tooth pinion at 1450 rev/min drives a 45-tooth wheel: 483 rev/min, from 1450 ÷ 3. Its wrong picks are 4350 rev/min, with the ratio multiplied, and 1450 rev/min, as if the gears kept the speed. Screen 3 shows the push at the mesh at 100% efficiency. The motor's 72.4 N m on the pinion's 0.04 m radius pushes its tooth with 72.4 ÷ 0.04 = 1811 N. The wheel's tooth is pushed back with the same 1811 N, but 0.2 m from its centre. So the wheel's torque is 1811 × 0.2 = 362 N m. Screen 4 asks the wheel's torque when the same 15 and 45-tooth pair has 20 N m on its pinion, with no loss: 60 N m. Its wrong picks are 6.7 N m, with the torque divided by the ratio, and 20 N m, as if the torque passed through unchanged. Screen 5 shows the power bar and the efficiency slider. At 100% the bar passes 11 kW straight through. At 95% it loses 550 W at the mesh and the pump shaft's torque drops from 362 N m to 344 N m. Screen 6 asks the power reaching the output shaft when 15 kW goes into a 4 : 1 gearbox of 96% efficiency: 14.4 kW. Its wrong picks are 60 kW, with the power multiplied by the ratio, and 15 kW, with the loss left out. Screen 7 turns on Second pair: the ratios multiply to 15, and the pump shaft turns at 96.7 rev/min with 981 N m. Screen 8 asks the output speed of a compound train with a 4 : 1 pair then a 6 : 1 pair, driven at 1440 rev/min: 60 rev/min, from a ratio of 24. Its wrong picks are 144 rev/min, with the ratios added to 10, and 360 rev/min, with only the first pair counted. Screen 9 turns on Belt. The belt dot keeps pace with both pulley rims, and the same ratio of 5 holds. Screen 10 asks a fan's speed when a 100 mm motor pulley at 1450 rev/min drives a 250 mm fan pulley by belt: 580 rev/min, from 1450 × 100 ÷ 250. Its wrong picks are 3625 rev/min, with the ratio upside down, and 1450 rev/min, as if a belt kept the speed. Screen 11 is a still drawing of a coupling joining a motor shaft to a pump shaft, three ways. In the first the two centre lines lie in one straight line. In the second they meet at an angle, which is angular misalignment. In the third they are parallel but offset, which is parallel misalignment. The angle and the offset are drawn exaggerated. Screens 12 and 13 mix it all. Screen 12 asks the torque on a winch drum shaft when a 4 kW motor at 960 rev/min drives it through a loss-free 4 : 1 gearbox: 159 N m. The drum turns at 240 rev/min, which is 25.13 rad/s, and 4000 ÷ 25.13 = 159 N m. Its wrong picks are 39.8 N m, the motor's own torque passed through unchanged, and 16.7 N m, from 4000 ÷ 240 with the speed left in rev/min. Screen 13 asks what is wrong when a pump's coupling and bearings run hot after a refit, and a check finds the two shafts parallel but one 0.5 mm higher. The right pick is parallel misalignment, since the centre lines must be one line. Its wrong picks are nothing, as if parallel shafts were aligned, and angular misalignment. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it. Each puzzle offers three answers, and a wrong pick is drawn so you can see where it goes wrong.
interactive.ignores: The teeth are drawn as simple blocks that touch at one point, on the circle where the gears meet. Real teeth are curved so they roll and slide smoothly, and often two pairs share the load at once. The efficiency is a setting, not worked out from the friction. A real gearbox's loss depends on its type, its load, its speed and its oil. The belt is drawn with no slip. A real belt creeps a little under load, so its driven pulley runs slightly slower than the ratio says. The belt's tension and its side pull on the bearings are not shown. The shafts are drawn rigid. A real shaft twists a little under torque, and how thick it must be is a calculation not shown here. The gears turn 50 times slower than real. The misalignment drawing exaggerates the angle and the offset.

explain.text:
A gear pair or a belt trades speed for torque. The slow shaft turns slower and pushes harder, by the same ratio. The power passes through almost unchanged, less a small loss to friction. A 5 : 1 reduction turns a motor's 1450 rev/min into 290 rev/min at the pump.

Two gears mesh only if their teeth are the same size. The teeth sit evenly round each rim. So a gear's tooth count goes with the distance round its rim, and so with its diameter. Where they meet, each tooth that passes on the pinion pushes one tooth past on the wheel. So the teeth of both gears move at the same speed at the mesh. The motor's 20-tooth pinion must turn five times to pass all 100 teeth of the wheel. So the wheel turns five times slower: 1450 rev/min in, 290 rev/min out. The input speed ÷ the output speed is the [[gear ratio]].[^1] For one pair it is the driven gear's teeth ÷ the driving gear's teeth, here 100 ÷ 20 = 5. A belt works the same way. If it does not slip, it moves at the speed of both pulley rims.[^2] So a belt's ratio is the driven pulley's diameter ÷ the driving pulley's diameter. An open belt turns both pulleys the same way. Two gears meshing on their outsides turn opposite ways.

Torque goes the other way, and the reason is at the mesh. In the gear pair drawn here, the pinion's teeth sit 0.04 m from its centre. The motor's 72.4 N m pushes them with 72.4 ÷ 0.04 = 1811 N. The pinion's tooth pushes the wheel's tooth with that 1811 N. By Newton's third law, the wheel's tooth pushes back just as hard, and that is the load the motor feels. The wheel's tooth sits 0.2 m from its centre, five times as far out. So the wheel's torque is 1811 × 0.2 = 362 N m, five times the motor's. Power is torque × angular speed, with the speed in radians per second.[^10] Five times the torque at a fifth of the speed is the same power. So a gearbox cannot make power. Friction turns a little of it into heat, so the power out is smaller than the power in.[^3] At an example efficiency of 95%, 11 kW in gives 10.45 kW out, and the pump shaft gets 344 N m. Two pairs in a row make a [[compound gear train]]. Its ratios multiply, so a 5 : 1 pair then a 3 : 1 pair give 15 : 1. Each pair loses its own share of the power too.

That is why the slow shaft is usually the thicker one. It carries almost five times the torque for the same power, and its coupling must carry that torque too. A coupling also needs its two shafts' centre lines in one straight line. Shafts that meet at an angle, or sit parallel but offset, have [[misalignment]]. It causes vibration, noise and heat, and wears out bearings, couplings and shafts early.[^5] The gear pair here is a simplified one, with rigid teeth and shafts. **A gear pair divides the speed by its ratio and multiplies the torque by it, while the power passes through less a small loss.**[^3]

analogy.text: Think of a step-down transformer. A 5 : 1 transformer divides the voltage by 5 and multiplies the current by 5. Volts × amps stay the same, less a small loss in the core and windings. A 5 : 1 gear pair divides the speed by 5 and multiplies the torque by 5, and torque × speed stays the same. The low-voltage side needs the thicker cable, because it carries the bigger current. The slow shaft needs to be thicker, because it carries the bigger torque.
analogy.breaks: A transformer works only on alternating current. A gear pair passes steady turning, which is more like direct current. A transformer also has no moving parts, while a gear pair's teeth push and slide, and that is where its loss comes from.

practice.text:
- Safe way first: isolate the motor and wait until every shaft has stopped before you take off a guard or touch a coupling, belt or gear. A belt or a gear mesh draws in fingers and clothing.
- Count the teeth, or measure the pulley diameters.
- Gear ratio = driven teeth ÷ driving teeth, or driven pulley diameter ÷ driving pulley diameter.
- Output speed = input speed ÷ the ratio.
- Input torque = power ÷ angular speed, with the speed in rad/s: rev/min × 2π ÷ 60.
- Output torque = input torque × the ratio × the efficiency.
- Power out = power in × the efficiency.
- For a compound train, multiply the ratios of each pair.
- Check that a coupling's two shafts lie in one straight line, with no angle and no offset.

**Rules of thumb:** the slow shaft carries the big torque, so it and its coupling are the strong ones. A gearbox passes power on. It never adds to it.

**Worked example:** a 7.5 kW motor at 960 rev/min drives a hoist through an 18-tooth pinion and a 36-tooth wheel. Take an example efficiency of 97%. The ratio is 36 ÷ 18 = 2, so the output turns at 960 ÷ 2 = 480 rev/min. 960 rev/min is 100.5 rad/s, so the motor's torque is 7500 ÷ 100.5 = 74.6 N m. The output torque is 74.6 × 2 × 0.97 = 144.7 N m. The power out is 7.5 × 0.97 = 7.28 kW.

**Common mistakes**
- Turning the ratio upside down. The bigger gear or pulley turns slower.
- Thinking a gearbox makes power because its torque goes up. The speed goes down by the same ratio.
- Leaving the speed in rev/min when working out torque from power.
- Adding the ratios of a compound train. They multiply.
- Taking parallel shafts as aligned. Their centre lines must be one line.
